A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, Simulated Students in Tutoring Dialogues: Substance or Illusion? Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–G support a reliable comparison, including material shifted across pages.

before.justification: v1 reports original student-simulation benchmarks, human evaluations, agreement measurements, and reward-function ablations in Tables 1–4, with additional analyses in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experimental and human-evaluation results, including the benchmark tables, reward ablations, and appendix analyses.

M1.justification: The seven metrics, student and evaluator models, SFT procedure, and offline DPO pipeline are unchanged. Appendix B.2 newly explains the development of the dialogue-act taxonomy, but the final definitions in Table 6 and associated prompts remain identical.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate student-turn simulation using the same Question-Anchored Tutoring Dialogues 2k dataset of UK middle-school mathematics tutoring. No additional datasets, populations, domains, or task scenarios are evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same SFT/DPO models and Zero-Shot, OCEAN, ICL, Reasoning, and Oracle comparators. Membership also remains unchanged in the human evaluation and reward ablation. Newly cited methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Both retain the 1,147/382/382 train/validation/test dialogue split, seven evaluation metrics, and training and decoding settings. Human evaluation still covers 190 turns across 38 dialogues with three evaluators. The ablation still uses a random 20% test subset.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds a brief case comparison of Reasoning, SFT, and real-student replies to illustrate differences in grammatical formality and punctuation. The reward ablations, label-distribution analyses, and performance-by-turn analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: The Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation reporting remains unchanged, with no added repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedures. The new discussion of unpredictable student behavior concerns interpretation rather than statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Quantitative results in the tables and figures are unchanged. Section 4.3 newly reports a qualitative example: Reasoning produces 'Yes, thanks — I'll enter D.', SFT produces 'yes thank you', and the real student says 'yes', supporting the added observation about prompting methods' formal language.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations for simulation, training, and evaluation are unchanged. The new suggestion that attainable metric scores may fall below one is an informal qualification, without a formal bound, derivation, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and main findings: reference-based evaluation of simulated student turns, benchmarking prompting and fine-tuning, and improved but still limited realism from fine-tuning and preference optimization.

C2.justification: Section 2.3 newly warns that training against LLM-evaluated metrics can exploit evaluator errors and recommends expert human checks. Section 4.2 qualifies the interpretation of poor scores by acknowledging an unknown attainable ceiling arising from randomness in student behavior.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents internal labeling and comparison with LLM labels when refining dialogue acts, including dropping an Other category and merging correct/incorrect math-answer categories during development. These disclose the origins of the unchanged taxonomy; hyperparameters, hardware, prompts, and resource access remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Appendix A expands discussion of prior work, including Cao et al. on student-response refinement, Song et al. on unlearning, Dou et al. on LLM-conducted realism tests, and Yuan et al. on the competence paradox. The central positioning around reference-grounded, turn-level simulation remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory additions, corrects wording such as the duplicated 'student student', and adds acknowledgments. The title, section organization, and overall narrative remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: Text reflow moves Tables 2 and 3 lower within PDF page 7 and changes surrounding page composition. The figures and tables retain their contents, captions, and designs; the later appendix pages match visually after accounting for pagination.

improvement.justification: The new explanation of dialogue-act development improves transparency, while the reward-hacking warning and attainable-score qualification make the evaluation's limitations clearer. Updated related work and the linguistic example add useful context. These provide modest gains in documentation and interpretation; the experimental evidence and its existing validation limits remain unchanged.
